title: From opinion to evidence: How Nishanth Kadiyala made AI creative testable
summary: Nishanth Kadiyala on building AI creative at Walmart Connect, using a golden dataset and A/B tests to settle quality debates and cut production to minutes.
body_markdown:
What makes an AI-generated advertisement good?


Ask a designer, a compliance lawyer, and a performance marketer, and you may get three different answers. One might focus on composition and brand consistency. Another might worry about misleading product imagery. The third wants to know whether the ad actually converts.


For **[Nishanth Kadiyala](https://www.growthbook.io/podcast/guests/nishanth-kadiyala) , Product Leader at HelloFresh and former ad tech leader at Walmart Connect** , the challenge was turning those competing judgments into a product that advertisers could trust—and into decisions supported by experimentation rather than opinion.


[On this episode of The Experimentation Edge](https://www.growthbook.io/podcast/episode/2-11) , Nishanth joins GrowthBook CMO Ashley Stirrup to share the lessons from building AI-powered creative automation for retail media, where the path from a promising prototype to a scalable product required far more than choosing the right generative model.


## The real problem wasn't just generating ads


At Walmart Connect, Nishanth worked across retargeting, dynamic creatives, and automated advertising.


The opportunity was especially significant for small and medium-sized advertisers. Large brands typically have creative teams and established advertising workflows. Smaller suppliers may have strong products but lack the resources to produce compelling display ads or navigate complex platform requirements.


AI offered a way to reduce that friction.


By starting with existing product detail pages, containing images and descriptive text, automated systems could help advertisers produce creative assets without beginning from scratch.


But the product still needed to satisfy very different groups: brand-conscious enterprises, performance-oriented smaller advertisers, legal stakeholders, and platform teams.


Building a useful system meant understanding which compromises were acceptable to each.


## From creative quality to creative acceptability


One of Nishanth's most important lessons was that creative quality is subjective.


Even professional designers can disagree about what looks good. The same designer might judge an advertisement differently on different days.


That makes subjective perfection a difficult product requirement.


The team shifted toward **creative acceptability** : a more operational definition of whether an ad was suitable to use.


Instead of endlessly debating visual details, they could evaluate practical questions. Does the image accurately represent the product? Is the environment appropriate? Does the ad avoid misleading claims or unauthorized branding? Does it meet the advertiser's needs?


These criteria made it possible to establish guardrails, improve models, and move toward reliable evaluation.


## Two levels of experimentation


Nishanth describes two important types of testing.


The first was conventional A/B testing. Could automatically generated creative perform as well as manually produced advertisements, even if the human-designed versions looked more polished?


This distinction mattered for internal buy-in. A creative that wins an aesthetic debate does not necessarily win a performance test.


The second layer involved evaluating the AI system itself.


Generative models are probabilistic. Repeating an instruction may not always produce the same output, which creates new challenges for quality assurance.


The Walmart Connect effort developed a representative evaluation dataset spanning more than 20,000 product items. Outputs could then be assessed against requirements such as accuracy, context, product fidelity, and compliance.


Rather than trusting a model because a few demonstrations looked promising, the team needed a repeatable way to evaluate performance across a vast catalog.


## Why smaller advertisers changed the product roadmap


Experimentation also revealed that smaller advertisers had different priorities from large brands.


For some, a simple product image on a plain background was already valuable. Others struggled not with design, but with the compliance requirements that determined whether their ads could run.


That led to a different product sequence: address moderation and guardrails, support straightforward creative production, and gradually introduce more sophisticated AI capabilities and user controls.


The broader lesson was to avoid building complexity before proving that customers need it.


Through an approximately 18-month development effort, Nishanth says the product progressed from its early stages to an open beta with more than 250 advertisers trying it.


**Creative production that previously took multiple weeks could be completed in minutes** , with the final output available in roughly five minutes.


The breakthrough was not simply a faster model. It was a process that combined automation, practical guardrails, and customer feedback.


## Bringing the lessons to HelloFresh


Nishanth now applies these principles from the advertiser's side at HelloFresh, where paid-social creative must work across brands, markets, languages, and changing customer preferences.


The challenge has shifted toward creative velocity, diversity, and excellence: generating enough meaningful variations to learn quickly without compromising brand requirements.


He also sees substantial potential for AI evaluation systems to improve the product development process itself, provided teams maintain strong datasets, clear standards, and disciplined experimentation.


## The lesson for product leaders


The shift from opinion to evidence is not about removing human judgment.


It is about making judgment more useful.


Human experts establish the standards. Evaluation systems identify whether those standards are being met. A/B testing reveals how creative performs in the real world. Customer feedback determines which problems deserve attention next.


For product leaders building AI capabilities, Nishanth's experience offers a clear principle: **make the system measurable before trying to make it perfect.**
